title: Multi-Sentence Argument Linking
research_question: Can a document-level model reliably link event roles to argument spans across sentence boundaries, and can a new large-scale benchmark support progress on this task?
methodology: The authors construct RAMS, a corpus of 9,124 annotated event instances covering 139 event types, from English news documents, with annotators selecting argument spans in a five-sentence window around each event trigger. They formulate multi-sentence argument linking as scoring combinations of an event, a semantic role, and a candidate span, using contextual representations and an explicit null candidate for unattested roles. Experiments compare several baselines and model variants on RAMS, examine sentence-distance effects and decoding constraints, and test transfer to AIDA, BNB, and GVDB datasets.

key_findings.finding: RAMS contains 9,124 annotated event instances from 3,993 news documents, with 139 event types, 65 role types, and 21,237 annotated argument links.

Although most RAMS arguments occur in the trigger sentence, arguments in neighboring sentences remain common enough to motivate document-level linking, with 82% of annotated arguments reported as sentence-local.
With gold trigger and gold argument spans supplied, the main model obtains 68.3 test F1, and type-constrained decoding using gold event types raises test F1 to 73.3.

When the system must consider all possible spans instead of being given gold argument spans, performance drops to about 6 F1, showing that candidate-span identification is a major unresolved end-to-end difficulty.
Performance on arguments one or two sentences from the trigger is comparable to performance on local arguments in the reported development-set analysis.
Pretraining on RAMS improves downstream AIDA argument-linking performance relative to training only on the smaller AIDA data.
Exact annotation boundaries are materially less consistent than coarse agreement about whether a role is present: pairwise exact span-boundary agreement is reported as 55.3%.

limitations: RAMS is derived from news articles rather than workplace email or enterprise chat, so its discourse structure and participant roles differ from the target domain.
The ontology describes event-semantic roles rather than workplace actions, decisions, assignees, deadlines, or action-to-deadline relations.
Implicit or group assignees are not annotated as dedicated phenomena.
Condition, negation, and modality scope are outside the annotation scheme.
The main high-scoring experiments assume gold argument spans and gold trigger spans, substantially simplifying exact evidence-span extraction.
End-to-end performance when all spans are candidates is very low relative to the gold-span setting.
Annotators are restricted to a five-sentence window and are instructed to choose the closest argument span for a role, which can exclude other valid discourse mentions.
Exact span-boundary agreement is only 55.3%, indicating substantial ambiguity for evaluations that demand exact argument evidence.
The five-sentence context design is based on event extraction in news and may not transfer to long email threads or enterprise-chat conversations.
raw_claims: RAMS is designed to study linking an event's semantic roles to argument spans that may occur outside the trigger sentence.
Each annotation example presents a five-sentence context centered on a typed event trigger.
Argument annotations are represented by token-level start and end offsets.
Annotators select the closest available span for each role when more than one mention could fill it.
The completed RAMS corpus contains 9,124 event instances and more than twenty-one thousand argument annotations.
Eighty-two percent of the annotated arguments are in the same sentence as their event trigger.
The model represents a potential link using the event, role, candidate span, and their contextual interactions.
A null argument option is used for roles that are not explicitly instantiated in the context.
The strongest main RAMS result relies on gold candidate argument spans and type-constrained decoding.
Removing the gold-span assumption causes a large performance decline.
Agreement on exact argument boundaries is markedly lower than agreement on whether an argument exists.
RAMS pretraining provides useful transfer to the smaller AIDA event-argument dataset.
The paper makes its RAMS data and implementation available through the project site.
